children: By Callum Keown and Janet H. Cho
United Airlines reported third-quarter earnings that reversed the stock's Tuesday rally.

The airline operator reported a slightly lower-than-expected adjusted profit of $2.54, and a 17.4% increase to $17.9 billion in operating revenue, despite a 62% rise in fuel costs. Wall Street had expected adjusted earnings of $2.57 per share on revenue of $17.9 billion, according to FactSet.

United stock fell 2% to $95.80 in late Tuesday trading, after closing up 2.3% at $97.77 in regular trading. Shares are down 13% this year, on pace for their worst year since 2022 when they fell nearly 14%, according to Dow Jones Market Data.
The sector has had a rough year as skyrocketing jet fuel prices have eaten into profits. Delta Air Lines is the only major airline stock in the green in 2026.

It's hard to see the sector launching a sustained rally without a sharp drop in jet fuel prices. "Any sustainable move higher for the group needs jet fuel to move meaningfully lower, in our view," UBS analyst Atul Maheswari said before United's earnings.

It's a good point. Brent crude oil prices are trading around $109 a barrel and jet fuel prices have more than doubled over the past year. Delta said it expects a $6 billion increase in fuel costs this year — and it's the only carrier to own a refinery to offset some of the impact of higher fuel prices. It's hard to see much upside with those dynamics.

Delta's stock closed up 2.7% at $76.66 on Tuesday, snapping a two-day losing streak and posting its largest percentage increase since Sept. 21. American Airlines climbed 3.7% on Tuesday, Southwest Airlines closed up 2.2%, and Alaska Air Group gained 1.1%.

Chicago-based United said its total revenue per available seat-mile rose 15.9% year over year, to $20.19, posting its "best quarterly unit revenue growth since the pandemic." It said its cost per available seat-mile rose 17.3%, to $18.56.
Delta Air Lines, which reported quarterly earnings on Oct. 9, said its total revenue per seat mile in the quarter grew 21% to $25.46. Delta's cost per available seat-mile rose 25% to $23.63.
United expects fourth-quarter operating revenue growth to be even higher than in the third quarter, projecting a 20% year-over-year increase to set a new record.

Compared with the year-ago third quarter, United reported "broad-based strength across all revenue streams," with premium revenue up 17%, basic economy revenue up 16%, loyalty revenue up 17%, and cargo revenue up 23%. Economy cabin revenue increased for the third straight quarter, with unit revenue up 17% year over year.

Delta posted record third-quarter revenue of $17.6 billion, up 16% year over year, but adjusted earnings of $1.72 per share missed earnings expectations. Delta also cut its full-year earnings guidance, to between between $5.10 and $5.60, down from $6.50 to $7.50 previously.
Delta's premium revenue grew 18% year over year, with double-digit unit revenue growth, and main cabin unit revenue grew 17%, loyalty revenue grew 18%, and cargo revenue grew 29%.

United said it increased capacity by 1.3% in the third quarter, while Delta has been trimming capacity. Delta Chief Commercial Officer Joe Esposito said it was reducing main cabin seats, with total seats growing less than 2% in the fourth quarter.

Delta also expects its December-quarter revenue to increase about 20%, but warned that fuel prices are expected to rise to $4.25 a gallon in the fourth quarter, up from $3.61 per gallon in the third quarter.
Delta expects to generate a pretax profit of $4.5 billion this year, while absorbing an eye-watering $6 billion increase in fuel costs, CEO Ed Bastian said.
Delta's stock is down 8.2% this month, but up 10.5% this year.
The problem for investors is that the stocks are subject to volatile energy markets. United is down 11% in October, coinciding with a 10% jump in Brent crude prices over the same period.

"The question is what can these airlines really say that drives these stocks sustainably higher from here?" UBS analyst Atul Maheswari said in a note Friday. "Given the macro/fuel concerns recently, we believe there is not a whole lot [they] can point to that drives meaningful sentiment shift positively."

United can still stop the descent, though, or even provide a brief uptick to the shares. But it needs to demonstrate stellar demand, strong enough to support higher airfares and help mitigate the surging fuel costs.
United management will host an earnings call to discuss results at 10:30 a.m. Eastern time on Thursday.
In July, United guided for earnings per share between $2.50 and $3.50. For the full year, Wall Street is looking for earnings per share of $7.94 — lower than United's own range between $9 and $11.

Both Southwest and Alaska Air Group, whose subsidiaries include Alaska Air, Hawaiian Airlines, and Horizon Air, report earnings on Wednesday. American Airlines, a Barron's stock pick in May, reports earnings on Thursday.
